The 9 Claude Code Settings Power Users Change on Day One

Vikas Sah

Claude Code asked me to confirm a file read forty-seven times in one morning before I gave up and went to the docs. That’s the moment I stopped accepting the defaults.

The defaults are conservative because Anthropic doesn’t know you yet. By week two they’re working against you. The 9 settings below are the ones I change on every fresh install, usually within the first hour. In the configs I’ve audited from other power users, six of these nine show up nearly every time.

If you skip the rest of this post and only do one thing, do #1.

[DIAGRAM: settings.json precedence — managed → CLI flags → local → project → user, top to bottom, with the “first match wins” arrow on the deny → ask → allow flow]

1. Pre-approve the tools you trust. Deny the ones you don’t.

Default permissions ask before nearly every tool call. That trains you to mash “yes” — exactly the muscle memory you don’t want when an agent is about to do something irreversible.

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Read",
      "Grep",
      "Glob",
      "Bash(npm test:*)",
      "Bash(git status)",
      "Bash(git diff:*)",
      "Bash(ls:*)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Bash(rm -rf:*)",
      "WebFetch(domain:*.internal)",
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env.*)",
      "Read(./secrets/**)"
    ]
  }
}

Rules evaluate deny → ask → allow, with the first match winning. Put a thoughtful 10-line allowlist in front of an explicit secrets denylist and you eliminate hundreds of confirmations a week without losing the safety net.

This is the single highest-leverage setting in Claude Code. If you haven’t customized it, you’re working with both hands tied.

2. Switch your default permission mode to plan

default mode prompts you for nearly every tool call — which is what generated the 47 confirmations from the opening of this post. plan mode is different: Claude Code walks through what it intends to do before doing it, you approve or steer the plan, and execution then runs without per-tool prompts.

{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "plan"
  }
}

Six modes exist as of v2.1: default, acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions. The auto and dontAsk modes are 2026 additions; auto uses a classifier to decide what's safe, which is great when you trust the classifier and a problem when you don't (the failure mode is "the agent does something you'd have caught in a permission prompt"). I use plan for unfamiliar repos and acceptEdits for repos I know cold.

Hedge: if your usual workflow is rapid throwaway scripts where reviewing a plan would slow you down, this isn’t your setting. Skip to #3.

3. Switch the output style off the default

The default output style narrates as it works. Helpful in week one. By month one, it’s noise — and it eats tokens you’re paying for.

{ "outputStyle": "Concise" }

I haven’t measured token savings carefully. In one 4-hour session the difference looked like roughly 15–20% to me, but the workload was unusually verbose; on a typical day the savings are smaller. The bigger win is signal-to-noise on screen.

4. Build a status line that tells you what you actually need to know

The default status line is empty. Power users put context-window utilization, current model, branch, and session cost there.

{
  "statusLine": {
    "type": "command",
    "command": "~/.claude/statusline.sh"
  }
}

The script can be 20 lines of bash. Mine shows context %, model, branch, and a cumulative cost number. The “wait, am I about to run out of context?” anxiety disappears the day you do this.

(I shipped a free quota status-bar tool earlier this year — drop it in if you’d rather not write your own.)

5. Add the minimum viable hook pair

Two hooks every project should have on day one: a PreToolUse secrets-scan that fires before Edit and Write, and a PostToolUse lint trigger that fires after.

{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "command": "~/.claude/hooks/secrets-scan.sh" }
    ],
    "PostToolUse": [
      { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "command": "npm run lint --silent || true" }
    ]
  }
}

The secrets-scan catches the “agent helpfully writes my API key into the README” failure mode before it ships. The lint trigger means you find out you broke a style rule the moment you broke it, not at PR review.

A note on cost: don’t put npm test in PostToolUse unless your test suite runs in under 3 seconds. On a real project, you'll want a fast linter or a targeted test subset (vitest related or equivalent). I learned this by sitting through a 90-second test run after every typo correction for half a day.

(I went deeper on hooks in Agent Hooks Are Claude Code’s Most Powerful Feature if you want the taxonomy.)

6. Extend your workspace scope

additionalDirectories lets Claude Code read sibling repos, shared config dirs, or your notes folder without you copy-pasting context into chat.

{
  "additionalDirectories": [
    "~/code/shared-configs",
    "~/notes/engineering"
  ]
}

Important nuance: this grants file access only, not config inheritance. The .claude/ config in those directories is not loaded — only the files. If you ever find yourself pasting paths from another repo into chat, that's the cue to set this.

7. Pin to the stable channel and floor your version

autoUpdatesChannel defaults to latest, which gets every release as it ships. The stable channel lags by a week or two and skips the "shipped, then was hotfixed twice in 48 hours" cycle.

{
  "autoUpdatesChannel": "stable",
  "minimumVersion": "2.1.104"
}

The minimumVersion floor prevents claude update from silently downgrading you below a known-good build. Useful when a teammate's machine ends up on an older version and Claude Code's behavior subtly drifts.

8. Drop the built-in git instructions

Claude Code injects a git/PR system-prompt block into every session. If you have your own opinionated git workflow (or you’re using a skill that handles commits), the built-in block is just context noise.

{ "includeGitInstructions": false }

You’ll save a few hundred tokens per session. On long sessions or large teams, that adds up.

9. Skip the WebFetch preflight if you’re behind a firewall

This is the one most people miss. Claude Code’s WebFetch tool runs a hostname-safety check that calls api.anthropic.combefore it lets a fetch through. If you're on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, or any setup with restricted egress, that preflight call fails — which makes WebFetch look broken even though it isn't.

{ "skipWebFetchPreflight": true }

Set this and WebFetch starts working again. If you're on a vanilla install with open egress, leave it off — the preflight is a real safety check, not theater.

The complete config

Drop this into ~/.claude/settings.json. Takes effect on your next Claude Code session.

{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "plan",
    "allow": [
      "Read", "Grep", "Glob",
      "Bash(npm test:*)", "Bash(git status)", "Bash(git diff:*)", "Bash(ls:*)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Bash(rm -rf:*)",
      "WebFetch(domain:*.internal)",
      "Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)", "Read(./secrets/**)"
    ]
  },
  "outputStyle": "Concise",
  "statusLine": { "type": "command", "command": "~/.claude/statusline.sh" },
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "command": "~/.claude/hooks/secrets-scan.sh" }
    ],
    "PostToolUse": [
      { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "command": "npm run lint --silent || true" }
    ]
  },
  "additionalDirectories": ["~/code/shared-configs", "~/notes/engineering"],
  "autoUpdatesChannel": "stable",
  "minimumVersion": "2.1.104",
  "includeGitInstructions": false,
  "skipWebFetchPreflight": true
}

What’s in your day-one config that’s not in mine?
